title: The Sower, the Storm, Legion, and Two Daughters
summary: Jesus travels preaching with the Twelve and a group of women who support the mission from their own means. He tells the parable of the sower and explains that the seed is the word of God, received differently by different hearts. Then come four acts of power: he calms a storm, frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, heals a woman who touches his cloak, and raises the daughter of Jairus.
story:
Luke has been showing who receives the kingdom and who rejects it: a centurion believes, a sinful woman is forgiven, and Pharisees and lawyers reject God's purpose for themselves (7:30). Now Jesus explains why the same message produces such different results, through a parable about soil. Hearing is the first half's theme: the sower's word is heard in many ways, the lamp must be seen, the disciples must take care how they listen, and Jesus' true family are those who hear God's word and do it.

The second half gathers stories that show Jesus' authority over every enemy of human life: the chaos of the sea, the demonic, chronic disease, and death itself. Faith and fear run through all of them. The disciples are asked where their faith is; the Gerasenes are gripped by fear; a woman comes forward trembling and is told her faith has healed her; Jairus is told not to fear but only believe. The chapter prepares for chapter 9, where the Twelve who have watched these things are sent out with the same power and authority, and where Peter at last answers the disciples' question from the boat, “Who is this?”
historical:
Only Luke describes the women traveling with Jesus during the Galilean ministry and names Joanna and Susanna; Mark mentions the women who had followed him and ministered to him in Galilee only when they appear at the cross (Mark 15:40-41), and Luke will mention them there too (23:49, 23:55). Mary called Magdalene was almost certainly from Magdala (Hebrew Migdal, ‘tower’), a prosperous fishing town on the western shore of the lake, north of Tiberias. Excavations begun in 2009 uncovered there a synagogue from before AD 70, one of the few known from the time of Jesus, with a carved stone block (the Magdala Stone) bearing one of the earliest known images of the temple menorah. Many scholars identify Magdala with the town Josephus calls Tarichaeae, a center for salting fish, though the identification is not certain.

Joanna's husband Chuza was Herod Antipas's epitropos, a steward or estate manager, a senior post in the household of the tetrarch who ruled Galilee from 4 BC to AD 39 from his new capital at Tiberias. The support for Jesus' mission therefore reached into the court of the man who had imprisoned John the Baptist and who would later question Jesus (23:6-12). Joanna reappears among the women at the empty tomb (24:10). Richard Bauckham (Gospel Women, 2002) has proposed that she is the Junia whom Paul greets as prominent among the apostles in Romans 16:7, Junia being a Latin name chosen for its likeness in sound to Joanna; the proposal is possible but unproven. Susanna is mentioned nowhere else.

The east side of the lake lay mostly in the region of the Decapolis, a league of cities with a largely Gentile, Greek-speaking population, which explains the herd of pigs. Jews did not raise pigs, which Leviticus 11:7 classes as unclean, and a later rule in the Mishnah forbids raising them anywhere (m. Bava Kamma 7:7). The name of the place varies between the Gospels and in the manuscripts: Gerasenes, Gadarenes (as in Matthew 8:28), and Gergesenes. Gerasa (modern Jerash in Jordan) was a major city about thirty-three miles southeast of the lake; Gadara (modern Umm Qais) about six miles southeast, with territory that may have reached the shore. Origen (Commentary on John, book 6, written in the 230s) already noticed that neither city lies on the lake and preferred Gergesa, an old town by the lake where local people pointed out a steep slope. Many connect Gergesa with Kursi on the eastern shore, where road builders in 1970 uncovered a large Byzantine monastery with a church, excavated from 1971 by Dan Urman and Vassilios Tzaferis; it seems to have been built around the fifth or sixth century to mark the site of this miracle. Matthew mentions two possessed men; Mark and Luke tell of one. The parallels to this chapter are Mark 4:1-25 and 4:35-5:43, and Matthew 8:23-34, 9:18-26, and 13:1-23.

Jews of the period knew of exorcists. Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist named Eleazar drawing out a demon through a man's nose in the presence of the future emperor Vespasian, using a ring and incantations attributed to Solomon, and ordering the demon to overturn a basin of water to prove it had left (Antiquities 8.45-49). The Gospels' exorcisms differ in having no rings, roots, or formulas: Jesus simply commands. Jewish writings of the period also describe evil spirits being bound in a place of confinement until judgment (1 Enoch 10:4-6, Jubilees 10:7-9), which is the background of the demons' dread of the Abyss.
cultural:
Farmers in Galilee sowed wheat and barley by scattering seed by hand from a bag. Gustaf Dalman and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, first published in German in 1947) argued that in Palestine sowing often came before plowing, so a sower would scatter seed over paths trodden across the field and over ground where thin soil covered limestone or where thorn roots lay hidden; others have questioned how general that practice was, but either way the losses in the parable are the ordinary risks of farming. A hundredfold harvest was extraordinary (compare Isaac's crop in Genesis 26:12). Luke gives only the hundredfold, where Mark has thirty, sixty, and a hundred. Parables, short stories or comparisons drawn from daily life (the Hebrew mashal covers proverbs, riddles, and allegories as well), were a familiar Jewish teaching form, and later rabbinic literature contains hundreds of them. They invited hearers to think and to decide.

Lamps were small clay bowls of olive oil with a wick, set on a stand or in a wall niche to light a one-room house. A bed or couch (klinē) raised off the floor could hide a lamp beneath it, as could a clay vessel turned over it. The point of verse 16 would be obvious to any householder: no one lights a lamp in order to hide it.

Several of the chapter's figures lived at the edges of purity law. Tombs, often caves cut in the hillside, were places of corpse impurity and were thought to be haunts of spirits. Pigs were unclean. According to Leviticus 15:25-27, a woman with a flow of blood outside her normal period was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted, and what she lay or sat on became unclean. Impurity was not sin; it barred a person from the temple and its sacred food, and how far it restricted ordinary life in Galilee, far from the temple, is debated. Amy-Jill Levine (Discharging Responsibility, 1996) has argued that the story itself says nothing about purity and that Christian preaching which makes Jesus overthrow Jewish purity law misreads it; the woman's plight in the text is illness, poverty from paying physicians, and twelve years of suffering. The fringe (kraspedon) of Jesus' cloak is probably the tassel that Numbers 15:38-39 commands Israelite men to wear at the corners of their garments as a reminder of God's commandments, a detail that presents Jesus as an observant Jew.

A synagogue leader (archisynagōgos) like Jairus was a respected layman responsible for the building and its services. The Greek Theodotus inscription, found in Jerusalem in 1913 and dated before AD 70, records a priest and synagogue leader who built a synagogue for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments. Mourning was loud and public, sometimes with hired mourners and flute players, and it began at once; the laughter of verse 53 comes from people who had already begun the funeral rites. A girl of twelve was on the edge of adulthood and marriageable age, which makes her death especially bitter for her parents.
literary:
The chapter has two halves. The first (verses 1-21) is about hearing: a summary of Jesus' travels, the parable, its explanation, sayings on the lamp and on listening, and the redefinition of Jesus' family. The words hear and word run through it, and it is framed by two statements about the word of God: the seed is the word of God (verse 11), and Jesus' mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (verse 21). Luke moves the episode of Jesus' family (Mark 3:31-35) so that it follows the parable and serves as its conclusion, and he softens it: nothing is said of the family thinking Jesus out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and his mother, whom Luke has already presented as one who hears and keeps God's word (1:38, 2:19, 2:51), is not excluded by the saying but included in it.

The second half (verses 22-56) is a series of four miracles, rising in intensity from nature to demons to disease to death. Each crosses a boundary: the disciples cross the lake into Gentile territory; Jesus meets a man living among tombs; an unclean woman touches him; he enters the room where a corpse lies. Luke keeps Mark's technique of framing one story inside another: the raising of Jairus's daughter is interrupted by the healing of the woman, and the delay costs the girl her life, or seems to. The two stories are tied by the number twelve (twelve years of bleeding, a girl of about twelve), by the word daughter (verse 48 and verses 42 and 49), by falling at Jesus' feet (verses 41 and 47), and by the language of saving and faith (verses 48 and 50).

Fear is a thread through the second half: the disciples are afraid after the calm (verse 25), the Gerasenes are seized with great fear (verse 37), the woman comes trembling (verse 47), and Jairus is told, “Do not be afraid; just believe” (verse 50). So is the question of identity. The disciples ask who Jesus is (verse 25), and the demon supplies an answer they cannot yet give: “Son of the Most High God” (verse 28), the title Gabriel used in 1:32. The man who was freed ends in the posture of a disciple, “sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind” (verse 35), and is sent home as the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis (verse 39). Luke lets two statements stand side by side: Jesus tells him to describe how much God has done, and he proclaims how much Jesus has done.

outline.t: The Twelve and the women who travel with Jesus
Why parables, and the sower explained
A lamp on a stand: take care how you listen
A woman healed by touching his cloak

doctrines.note: The seed is the word of God (verse 11), and its fruitfulness depends on how it is heard. Revelation is given and is meant to be seen, like a lamp on a stand (verse 16), but it can be snatched away, received shallowly, or choked. What is hidden will be made known (verse 17), so the call is to take care how one listens (verse 18).

Jesus proclaims the good news of the kingdom of God (verse 1), and its mysteries are given to the disciples (verse 10). The four miracles show what that reign looks like when it arrives: the sea, the demons, disease, and death all yield to the King's word.

Jesus asks the disciples in the storm where their faith is (verse 25), tells the woman her faith has healed her (verse 48), and tells Jairus to believe even after news of death (verse 50). Faith is trust in Jesus that reaches out to him and holds when circumstances say it is too late.

Only Luke ends the explanation of the good soil with the words “by persevering produce a crop” (verse 15). The rocky soil believes for a season and falls away in testing (verse 13). Fruit is the mark of true hearing, and it comes through endurance over time.

Jesus names a deeper kinship: his mother and brothers are those who hear God's word and do it (verse 21). The community of disciples becomes a family that includes the formerly unclean and outcast, as when Jesus calls the healed woman “Daughter” (verse 48).

words.note: Diakoneō, to serve, wait at table, minister, provide for. It occurs 37 times in the New Testament and eight times in Luke. In verse 3 the women ‘were ministering’ to Jesus and the Twelve out of their own means, that is, they supported the mission with money, food, and practical care. The same verb describes Jesus' own role: “I am among you as one who serves” (22:27). Later the related noun diakonos came to name an office (deacon), but here it describes service, not an office.

Mustērion, mystery, secret. It occurs 28 times in the New Testament, only once in each Synoptic Gospel (here, Mark 4:11, Matthew 13:11), and most often in Paul. In the New Testament it does not mean a puzzle to be solved by cleverness, but part of God's plan once hidden and now revealed to those he chooses (Romans 16:25-26). Luke's plural, the mysteries of the kingdom, refers to the truths about God's reign that Jesus' teaching discloses to disciples.

Hupomonē, perseverance, patient endurance. It occurs 32 times in the New Testament but only twice in the Gospels, both in Luke (here and 21:19, “By your patient endurance you will gain your souls”). Luke alone adds it to the explanation of the good soil. It names staying power under trial, the opposite of the rocky soil that falls away in the time of testing (verse 13).

Epistatēs, master, one set over others. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, all in Luke, always in the vocative as an address to Jesus and almost always from the disciples (5:5, 8:24 twice, 8:45, 9:33, 9:49; once from lepers, 17:13). Where Mark has teacher or rabbi, Luke often uses this word, which suits Greek-speaking readers and expresses respect for an authority.

Legiōn, legion, a Latin loanword. It occurs four times in the New Testament (here, Mark 5:9 and 5:15, Matthew 26:53). A Roman legion had about five to six thousand soldiers. The name conveys vast number and organized, overwhelming force. Some readers of Mark, such as Ched Myers (Binding the Strong Man, 1988), have heard in it a hint of Roman military occupation, noting that the legion stationed in the region, the Tenth Fretensis, used a boar among its emblems; others think the name simply expresses multitude.

Abussos, the abyss, the bottomless deep. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, seven of them in Revelation. In the Greek Old Testament it translates tehom, the deep waters (Genesis 1:2). In Jewish thought of the period it was also a prison where rebellious spirits were held until judgment, as in Revelation 20:1-3; Paul uses it for the realm of the dead (Romans 10:7). The demons' plea (verse 31) shows they know Jesus has authority to consign them there before the appointed time.

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal, make whole. It occurs 106 times in the New Testament, 17 in Luke, and four times in this chapter, each with a different shade: those beside the path do not believe and are not saved (verse 12); the possessed man was healed, literally saved (verse 36); the woman's faith has healed, literally saved, her (verse 48); and Jairus is promised that his daughter will be healed, or saved (verse 50). Luke uses one word for rescue of body and of soul because Jesus brings both.

christ:
The disciples' question in the boat is the chapter's question: “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!” (verse 25). In the Old Testament it is God who rules the raging sea: “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them” (Psalm 89:9), and in Psalm 107 sailors caught in a storm cry to the LORD and “He calmed the storm to a whisper” (Psalm 107:29). Jesus does in person what the psalms say only God does. He rebukes the wind as he rebukes demons (4:35, 4:39), treating the storm as one more power opposed to God's reign. His sleep in the boat may recall Jonah asleep in the storm, but where Jonah had to be thrown overboard, Jesus stills the sea himself.

The demons name him Son of the Most High God and tremble, while the disciples do not yet know what to call him. Power goes out from him when a desperate woman touches him, and his word calls a dead girl back to life. What sets him apart is not only power but the way he uses it. He stops to find a woman who hoped to go unnoticed and gives her public restoration and a new name, Daughter. He remembers that a girl just raised from death needs something to eat. He sends the freed man home rather than taking him along, so that a Gentile region hears what God has done. And he treats the dead girl as sleeping (verse 52), a way of speaking the early church adopted for believers who die in hope of resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14).

The parable, too, points to him. He is the sower whose word is the word of God, and the lamp saying anticipates the time when what is now hidden in his ministry will be disclosed. The chapter's four miracles preview the whole of his work: authority over creation, victory over Satan's kingdom, healing that makes the unclean whole, and resurrection. They are signs that the one who will himself die and be raised holds the keys of death.
interpretation:
The parable of the sower has invited allegory from the start, since Jesus himself explains it point by point. The church fathers applied the soils to the soul's reception of the word: Cyril of Alexandria in his homilies on Luke and Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 15) both preached it as a warning about riches, pleasures, and inconstancy. The storm became a figure of the church in the world. Augustine (Sermon 63) told his hearers that when they are provoked to anger the wind is blowing and Christ is asleep in them, because they have forgotten him, and that they must wake him by recalling his words. Eusebius (Church History 7.18, early fourth century) reports that at Caesarea Philippi, said to be the home of the woman healed of bleeding, a bronze statue of a kneeling woman and a man stretching out his hand to her stood outside her house, and that he had seen it. The apocryphal Acts of Pilate (in its present form from about the fourth century) gives her the name Bernice, and in the Latin West the name became Veronica, whom later legend connected with the cloth bearing Christ's face on the way to the cross.

Mary Magdalene's introduction in verse 2 became entangled with the sinful woman of chapter 7. Gregory the Great (Homily 33, probably 591) read her seven demons as all the vices and identified her with the woman who anointed Jesus' feet, a reading that shaped Western art and devotion until the Roman calendar reform of 1969 separated them; the Eastern churches never made the identification and honor her as a myrrh-bearer and equal to the apostles. Second- and third-century writings outside the New Testament, such as the Gospel of Mary and the Gospel of Philip, gave her a prominent role among the disciples. The historical reading of Luke 8:2 is simpler: she was healed of severe demonic affliction and became a follower, and Luke nowhere links her to sexual sin.

Modern study of the parables began with Adolf Jülicher (Die Gleichnisreden Jesu, 1888-1899), who argued that each parable makes a single point and that the allegorical explanations were the early church's work. C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, 1947) read the sower as Jesus' assurance that despite losses the kingdom's harvest would be abundant, and Jeremias judged the explanation to be a later application. Others, including Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008), have answered that Jewish parables often carried allegorical features and that there is no good reason to deny Jesus an explanation of his own story. The Gerasene story provoked a famous Victorian debate: the scientist Thomas Henry Huxley, arguing with W. E. Gladstone in the journal The Nineteenth Century (his essay The Keepers of the Herd of Swine, 1890), pressed the moral problem of destroying another man's property, and Bertrand Russell repeated the objection in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927). Liberation and empire-critical readers, following Ched Myers on Mark (1988), read Legion as Roman occupation personified. Amy-Jill Levine (1996, and with Ben Witherington III in The Gospel of Luke, 2018) has challenged interpretations of the bleeding woman that set Jesus against Jewish purity law.

In art, Rembrandt's The Storm on the Sea of Galilee (1633), his only seascape, shows the disciples struggling with the sail and Jesus being roused; it was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston in 1990 and has not been recovered. The healing of the bleeding woman appears in early Christian catacomb painting in Rome. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 8:26-39 in Year C after Pentecost, and 8:1-3 closes the reading of 7:36-8:3 in both the Revised Common and Roman lectionaries.
text:
The most visible difference between English Bibles in this chapter is the place name in verses 26 and 37. The papyrus P75 (about AD 200), Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae read Gerasenes, which most modern editions and versions print. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Regius (L), with a number of other manuscripts, read Gergesenes, the reading Origen recommended on geographical grounds. The majority of later Byzantine manuscripts read Gadarenes, as in Matthew 8:28, and the King James Version follows them. Scribes seem to have adjusted the name toward the parallels or toward places they knew, and the same three names vary in the manuscripts of Mark and Matthew as well.

In verse 43 the words about the woman having spent all her living on physicians are missing from P75 and Codex Vaticanus; most other manuscripts include them. Westcott and Hort omitted them, some earlier Nestle editions did too, and the current Nestle-Aland text prints them (the BSB translates them). They may be a scribal addition from Mark 5:26, or an original clause dropped by a few copies. In verse 3 the text most editors print says the women provided for ‘them’, Jesus and the Twelve, while other manuscripts and the Textus Receptus have ‘him’ (the King James Version's ‘ministered unto him’), probably under the influence of Matthew 27:55 and Mark 15:41. In verse 45 the King James Version has a longer form of Peter's reply (‘the multitude throng thee and press thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?’), which borrows from Mark 5:31 and is absent from the earliest manuscripts; in verse 48 it adds ‘be of good comfort’, found in later manuscripts under the influence of Matthew 9:22.

Verse 10 quotes Isaiah 6:9 in a shortened form. Mark 4:12 continues with the words ‘lest they turn and be forgiven’, where the Hebrew of Isaiah 6:10 speaks of being healed; Luke omits that clause entirely. Translations also differ in verse 10 over the Greek hina, rendered ‘so that’ (purpose) by most versions, though some interpreters read it as introducing the fulfillment of Scripture, as in ‘so that it may be as Isaiah said’.

teach.big: The word of God bears fruit in those who hear it with an honest heart and hold on to it, and the Jesus who speaks that word has authority over nature, demons, disease, and death.

outline.t: The mission of the kingdom is carried by a community of the healed, women and men alike, who give what they have.
God's word is scattered generously; the harvest will surpass all the losses.
The same word meets four kinds of hearers; what matters is an honest heart that holds on and perseveres.
Revelation is given to be shown, not hidden, and how we listen determines whether we gain more or lose even what we think we have.
Jesus' family is defined by hearing and doing God's word, and that door is open to anyone.
Jesus rules the chaos that terrifies us, and he asks where our faith is when the storm comes.
No one is too bound, too unclean, or too far gone for Jesus to set free, and freedom can cost a community something it would rather keep.
Jesus stops for the one who hoped to go unnoticed, and turns a secret healing into public restoration and belonging.
When the news says it is too late, Jesus says do not fear, only believe; death is not the last word in his presence.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The parable of the sower is sometimes preached as a sorting device for labeling other people as rocky or thorny soil. Jesus tells it to his own hearers, and verse 18 turns it back on the listener: take care how you listen. It is also misread as teaching that the rocky soil lost a salvation it once had, or, on the other side, as proving that such people never believed at all. Luke says they believed for a season (verse 13); the parable's point is that only persevering faith bears fruit, and teachers from different traditions on perseverance can agree on that without forcing the parable to settle their debate.

The storm is often preached as a promise that faith will prevent or quickly end life's storms. The disciples had Jesus in the boat and still faced a storm, and his rebuke concerns their fear, not their asking. With the Gerasene man, avoid sensational speculation about demons, and avoid dismissing the story as ancient misdiagnosis of mental illness; Luke distinguishes the demonic from illness elsewhere (for example 6:18, 7:21), and the story's point is Jesus' authority and the man's restoration. With the bleeding woman, avoid the common claim that Jesus defied or abolished Jewish purity law by being touched: the law did not forbid touching her, the text never mentions purity, and the fringe she touched was itself a sign of Torah observance. Finally, do not make the woman's touch into a technique, as if contact with holy objects produces healing. Jesus insists on meeting her, and he says her faith, not the fringe, has made her well.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will touch people living with chronic illness, especially women with conditions that are hidden, embarrassing, or dismissed by doctors, and people who have spent their savings on treatment without relief. Jesus' attention to her story, told in front of everyone (verse 47), dignifies what others overlooked. The Gerasene story will touch families of people with serious mental illness and addiction; teach it without equating mental illness with demon possession and without suggesting that such suffering reflects a lack of faith, and keep a path to medical and professional help visible. The raising of Jairus's daughter will press on parents who have lost children, and on those who prayed for a child's healing that did not come. Jesus' words, “Do not be afraid; just believe”, are not a promise that every sick child will recover; they are an invitation to trust him in the face of death, whose final answer is resurrection.

hard.q: Does Jesus tell parables to keep people from understanding?
hard.a:
Verse 10 quotes Isaiah 6:9, where God sends Isaiah to a people who will hear without understanding. Read on its own, it can sound as if Jesus deliberately hides the truth to keep people out. The objection has been pressed hard. Adolf Jülicher (1888-1899) thought the saying could not come from Jesus, whose parables were meant to make things clear, and attributed it to the early church's attempt to explain why most of Israel did not believe. Readers outside the church have seen in it an exclusive, sectarian message for insiders only.

Interpreters respond in several ways. Many read it in the light of Isaiah and of the whole chapter: parables reveal and conceal at once. To those who come to Jesus and ask, as the disciples do in verse 9, they open up; to those who have already closed their hearts, they remain only stories, and that result is itself a form of judgment on refusal, as it was in Isaiah's day. Joachim Jeremias argued that the saying originally applied to Jesus' teaching as a whole, not to parables specifically, and that the underlying Aramaic might mean that for outsiders everything remains a riddle unless they repent. Others note that Luke shortens Mark's version and omits the clause about not being forgiven, which softens the note of intended exclusion. Theologians in the Reformed tradition stress God's sovereign purpose in revealing and hiding (compare 10:21), while others stress human responsibility, pointing to verse 18's warning to take care how you listen. The verses that immediately follow, about a lamp meant to be seen and hidden things that will be disclosed (verses 16-17), show that the goal of Jesus' teaching is light, not concealment.

hard.q: Was it right for Jesus to allow the demons to destroy a herd of pigs that belonged to someone else?
hard.a:
The objection is moral and has a long history. Thomas Henry Huxley (The Keepers of the Herd of Swine, 1890) argued that the wanton destruction of other people's property is wrong, and that the Gospel writers show no awareness of the problem. Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) added that it was unkind to the pigs, and that an all-powerful Jesus could simply have made the demons go away. Some historical critics also doubt the incident, suspecting a folk tale about tricked demons that grew around an exorcism.

Responses begin with the text. Jesus does not send the demons into the pigs; he permits their request (verse 32), and it is the demons who destroy the herd, which fits the Gospels' picture of evil as destructive of whatever it touches. W. E. Gladstone, answering Huxley, argued that the swine-keepers, if they were Jews, were breaking the law by keeping them, though most commentators think the region was Gentile and that the argument does not hold. Many interpreters see the stampede as visible proof to the man and the town that the demons had truly left, a demonstration of their number and malice. Others weigh the value of one man's sanity and freedom against the value of a herd, and note that the townspeople themselves drew the same comparison and chose the pigs, which is the story's sharper challenge. Some readers take the episode symbolically as the expulsion of unclean forces from the land, with Legion evoking Rome. Christians who share the concern for animals need not deny that the loss was real; the Gospels present it as part of the cost of a man's deliverance. A reader who does not accept the reality of demons will judge the story differently, and should know that the dispute turns partly on that prior question.

observe: Name the women Luke mentions in verses 2-3, and say what each had experienced and what they were doing.
What happens to the seed in each of the four soils, and how does Jesus explain each one?
What did the people of the region find when they came out to see the healed man, and how did they respond?
interpret: Why do you think Luke places the saying about Jesus' true family right after the parable of the sower?
Why did Jesus insist on finding the woman who touched him instead of letting her slip away healed?
What does the storm story reveal about who Jesus is, in light of Psalms 89 and 107?
apply: Which of the four soils best describes how you have received God's word in this season of your life, and what would it take to hold on and persevere?
The people of the region asked Jesus to leave because they were afraid. What might we prefer to keep, even at the cost of sending Jesus away?
Jesus told Jairus, ‘Do not be afraid; just believe’, when the news was worst. Where do you need to hear that word today?
